💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.
  • According to recent reports, beginning in early 2024, I spent two years building a start-up as a co-founder and its Chief Content Officer.
  • Industry observers note that I left not because the mission wasn’t worthwhile or the work was no longer meaningful, but because the cumulative psychological demands crossed a line I was no longer willing to cross.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.

According to recent reports, beginning in early 2024, I spent two years building a start-up as a co-founder and its Chief Content Officer. It was an interesting, intense, exciting, and frustrating experience. As I reflect on it, I feel an immense feeling of satisfaction at how much we accomplished. At the same time, I also feel a sense of lost opportunity. Why? Because in early 2026, I chose to leave the company.

Industry observers note that I left not because the mission wasn’t worthwhile or the work was no longer meaningful, but because the cumulative psychological demands crossed a line I was no longer willing to cross. The current start-up culture often frames departures like mine as a failure of sorts, whether a lack of vision or perseverance or resilience. I’m sure as a way to justify the psychological and emotional costs that are incurred for those who choose to pay those costs, regardless of how high they run. For me, however much time and psychological capital I had invested (not to mention a fair amount of financial capital), I could no longer continue to pay those costs, even though the financial ROI might have paid for those costs down the road.

This is the first in a series about what I learned. These articles reflect my experience and interpretation; my former co-founders may understand parts of our shared experience differently. This article introduces you to the seven psychological challenges that I experienced that build slowly, inside founders at first, and they compound, but, unfortunately, not like interest.

In a recent development, uncertainty is not an occasional stressor in a start-up. It is the steady drip, drip, drip that fills every waking hour. Questions about market fit, funding, and product decisions can remain unresolved for months. And every moment triggers an unending sense of urgency.

It has been revealed that our brains crave familiarity, predictability, and control. But there is nothing familiar, predictable, or controllable about a start-up. The constant mental activity, emotional rollercoaster, and cortisol bursts that founders experience due to this uncertainty can lead to persistent hypervigilance and, in time, the erosion of everything that is required to build a tech giant, including perspective, patience, resilience, and, for me, a basic enjoyment of the work.

In a recent development, research on entrepreneurship has reported a strong relationship between uncertainty and stress in the start-up process. And it’s not a byproduct of founding a start-up; rather, it’s baked fully into the experience.

Sources indicate that there’s a saying that “business is just business,” but in the start-up world, business is personal. Founders invest their identity in the business and risk their fortunes and futures, all on an opportunity that, statistically, has little chance of being realized. When the tech giant struggles, it can feel like you are struggling. When traction is slow, it can feel like it’s your fault. That creates a boiling cauldron of stress.

It has been revealed that I worked “pedal to the metal” for almost two years. As Chief Content Officer, I felt that if I slowed down, the manufacturer would grind to a halt. My co-founders did their part, but without content, our company was dead in the water. I loved creating and seeing tangible results. For a long time, I thrived on the pressure. Yet every morning, as other stressors related to the start-up accumulated, the weight on my shoulders got heavier and heavier.

Start-ups reward urgency and intensity. But intensity doesn’t always play nice with productivity. When exhaustion becomes your baseline, you lose the ability to notice how impaired you are. Sleep goes south. The ability to focus declines. Irritability becomes the rule, not the exception. Relationships get tense, and conflicts increase. Eventually, many founders feel emotionally flat, as if the battery ceases to get recharged.

Recent findings suggest that research on entrepreneurial burnout highlights the toll of sustained emotional demands and dwindling resources. From the inside, burnout rarely unveils itself. It disguises itself as dedication.

According to recent reports, when you’re self-funding, every expense feels like a part of you is being lost, because it is. Even if you can afford it, watching money go out month after month with little coming in wears on you.

Among the self-employed, financial concerns strongly shape psychological well-being. In a start-up, financial anxiety can disrupt sleep, intensify conflict, or narrow what you’re willing to try.

My private practice eased the financial pressure I felt and gave me the freedom to leave. My co-founders were at different stages of their careers and faced different financial pressures. My own financial security gave me options they didn’t have.

We were bootstrapping, trying to cover expenses each month while waiting for revenue. As the app fell further behind schedule, revenue slipped further into the future. The company was on the clock, and the clock was always ticking down. We all felt it acutely.

Recent findings suggest that under pressure, people change their behavior. They make things simpler even when complexity is necessary. They think less deliberately and fall back on impulse and habit. Time pressure also reduces creativity, precisely when innovation is most needed.

It has been revealed that start-ups are cognitively heavy because everything connects to everything else. Product, marketing, revenue, runway, and hiring also impact each other. It can feel like a Möbius strip.

In a recent development, my formal role was Chief Content Officer. In practice, because of my relevant expertise and experience, I was involved in nearly every aspect of the business—strategy, design, marketing, sales, and finance, including areas where I knew very little.

Role overload felt like wearing a weight vest all day. Research on entrepreneurial role stressors helped me understand why the work had become so unsatisfying. Over time, I felt I was carrying more than my share, and it became a witch’s brew of inequity and resentment.

Industry observers note that together, these pressures make it harder for founders to accurately judge how the start-up is doing and when change is needed. Chronic uncertainty, identity-linked stress, emerging burnout, financial threat, time pressure, and role overload create the perfect psychological storm for biased judgment.

Industry observers note that optimism bias starts with a belief every founder must have: Something unlikely—building a successful and sustainable company—will happen. The danger comes when that belief keeps you underestimating timelines, costs, and obstacles long after the evidence suggests otherwise.

Confirmation bias protects that optimism. Founders begin to give more weight to information that supports the current path. Delays become temporary setbacks and structural problems are seen as execution concerns.

It has been revealed that loss aversion makes walking away feel like accepting a personal loss. The research on this is robust. Time, money, reputation, and identity are already invested. The more you’ve put in, the harder it is to acknowledge that it’s time to cut your losses and get out.

Sources indicate that I also saw how easily confidence can outpace competence. A few articles, videos, and conversations could harden into strong opinions about complex decisions. That included areas where I was learning as I went. The Dunning-Kruger effect helps explain why people with limited expertise can overestimate what they know. I think of this as “YouTube expertise,” the tendency to mistake familiarity with a subject for actual expertise and experience. When that happens, overconfidence and rigidity of thinking become more likely.

In a recent development, from the inside, it feels like conviction, clarity, and leadership. From the outside, it just looks like poor judgment. Once those biases take hold, course correction becomes psychologically very difficult. Changing direction can mean admitting that the decisions you’ve defended for months may have been wrong. My Ph.D. in psychology certainly didn’t inoculate me against cognitive biases.

According to recent reports, I haven’t regretted co-founding the organization for a minute. I loved pursuing big goals. I enjoyed being pushed outside my comfort zone. I took immense pleasure in bringing ideas to life. What I regret is how easily I came to see the psychological cost as part of the job. I told myself the sacrifice was worth it, with that proverbial pot of gold at the end of the rainbow (aka unicorn status), and that pushing through was always the virtuous route to take.

Sources indicate that many start-ups don’t struggle because the idea is wrong or they lack funding. They falter because psychological and interpersonal costs build steadily and reach a tipping point where they far outweigh the benefits. Leaving after two years was the healthiest decision I could make. When I gave my Notice of Separation to my co-founders, the dominant emotion I felt was relief. That relief told me everything I needed to know. And what it told me was that walking away was the right decision for me.

Breaking: Tesla Cybertruck’s already impressive turning radius gets even tighter

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (910 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla is rolling out an patch that makes the Cybertruck turn even tighter, improving on what was already one of the best turning radiuses you can get in a full-size pickup.
  • It only works on 2027 model year Cybertrucks, and Tesla looks to stop building the truck by the end of next summer.
  • Tesla’s official Cybertruck account posted a short drone video early Saturday showing a truck doing circles in a parking lot, with a “before” and “after” comparison of its turning path.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla is rolling out an patch that makes the Cybertruck turn even tighter, improving on what was already one of the best turning radiuses you can get in a full-size pickup.

But there’s a catch. It only works on 2027 model year Cybertrucks, and Tesla looks to stop building the truck by the end of next summer.

Tesla’s official Cybertruck account posted a short drone video early Saturday showing a truck doing circles in a parking lot, with a “before” and “after” comparison of its turning path. “Even tighter turns now rolling out to fresh Cybertrucks,” the account wrote.

In a follow-up post, Tesla mentioned the improvement requires software version 2026.44 or newer and “only applies to model year 2027 Cybertrucks.”.

It's not the size … it's how you maneuver itEven tighter turns now rolling out to fresh Cybertrucks pic.twitter.com/FuNoox4ax0.

Tesla didn’t share a latest turning circle figure. In the video, the “after” circle is visibly smaller than the “before” one by what looks to be at least a foot.

It has been revealed that the Cybertruck’s maneuverability comes from its rear-wheel steering paired with steer-by-wire. At low speeds, the rear wheels turn opposite to the fronts, which shrinks the space the truck needs to make a U-turn. We’ve been tracking the Cybertruck’s four-wheel steering since the prototype days, when Tesla was showing it off in parking garages.

Even before this enhancement, the results were impressive. Tesla’s owner’s manual lists the Cybertruck’s curb-to-curb turning circle at about 43.5 ft (13.25 m). That beats the Ford F-150 Lightning at roughly 47.8 ft and the Rivian R1T at 44.9 ft, and it’s within about 4 ft of a Model Y. Not bad for a 6,600-lb truck that’s nearly 19 feet long.

Recent findings suggest that and Tesla always stated there was more to come. At launch, the rear wheels turned only about 3 degrees. In early 2024, a Tesla engineer said a software update would push that to 10 degrees, and Elon Musk said the tech giant had improvements in the works to “tighten the turning circle significantly.”.

It has been revealed that tesla hasn’t said whether this update delivers the full 10 degrees, or why it’s limited to 2027 trucks. If it comes down to hardware, owners of earlier Cybertrucks who were counting on this as an over-the-air upgrade are out of luck.

Credit where it’s due. The turning circle is one of the best things about the Cybertruck, and anyone who has driven one knows it. Steer-by-wire combined with rear-wheel steering is real engineering, and other vehicles are just starting to get that combo a couple years after Cybertruck had it. Making it even better is a nice update.

But it’s hard to get excited about it.

It has been revealed that and 39.4 feet turning circle for the Cadillac Escalade which also has rear wheel steering. As does the iX5 (39.7'), MB GLC (36.7') and EQS (35.8'), the Lucid Gravity (38.4), Hummer 37.4', Cayenne (38.4) and a around two dozen other vehicles on the market today. So maybe this is not such big news after all?

Recent findings suggest that earlier this month, Musk confirmed that Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at Gigafactory Texas to make room for Cybercab. He has since pushed the end date to the end of summer 2027 to work through an “order backlog.” We estimate Tesla is delivering about 7,000 to 8,000 Cybertrucks a quarter, roughly 12% of the 250,000 units a year it planned for.

So Tesla is improving a 2027 model year truck that it will stop making next summer. And since Tesla now only sells the $109,990 Cyberbeast, the people getting this upgrade are the few still buying the most expensive Cybertruck in its final months. It does nothing about what actually sank the truck: pricing that never came close to the $39,900 promised in 2019, range and towing that fell short, and a design most truck buyers never warmed up to.

Industry observers note that it’s a cool engineering flex on a product with an expiration date. If Tesla had delivered this kind of polish on the $40,000 truck it promised, would we be writing the Cybertruck’s obituary right now?

Audi Files Patent Application for Physical Buttons That Fold Out From Behind a Touchscreen

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Physical buttons have a lot going for them.
  • In a recent development, as CarMoses first discovered, Audi has filed for a patent application that describes a motorized switch bar, which pivots out from behind the display’s lower edge.
  • For those who do want the physical buttons, there are plenty of reasons to get excited.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Physical buttons have a lot going for them. They’re easy to find by feel, satisfying to use, and generally pretty good at staying wherever the automaker installed them. Well, it seems Audi has an idea that would change that last part: it involves hiding the buttons behind a touchscreen, then deploying them when needed.

In a recent development, as CarMoses first discovered, Audi has filed for a patent application that describes a motorized switch bar, which pivots out from behind the display’s lower edge. The screen stays fixed, while the physical controls swing into position beneath it. Interestingly, when stowed, the bar apparently has an on-screen counterpart with the same functions lined up in the same order, so those who don't want physical buttons can avoid them entirely.

For those who do want the physical buttons, there are plenty of reasons to get excited. First, Audi notes in its patent documents with the German government that the switches can deploy at startup, via voice controls, or via gestures. Moving the controls from the screen to the physical switches also provides more total screen room for people. (In one example, the physical bar deploys when a movie opens, leaving more room for the video.).

In a recent development, ultimately, this could be a great way to meet the demands of more people. Designers love a clean dashboard without physical buttons and switches. Plenty of drivers really love having that switchgear. This system allows owners to pick whatever they want on the fly.

The timing makes plenty of sense too. Audi has openly mentioned that it views moving toward more mechanical controls as the right direction. Of course, adding extra complexity to the once-simple idea of buttons also can increase the cost down the line when it comes time for repairs, but even so, this idea is certainly a fascinating solution to a very modern problem.

Mysterious volcanic rock discovered in the Mariana Trench

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (821 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, space exploration tends to suck up most of the oxygen when it comes to venturing out into the unknown.
  • That absurd depth and bone-crushing pressure make Challenger Deep brutally difficult to study.
  • Industry observers note that using the remotely operated Jason/Medea submarine robot, the team documented evidence of pyroclastic rocks (the shattered debris of violent eruptions) on the trench wall some 20,000 feet below the surface.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, space exploration tends to suck up most of the oxygen when it comes to venturing out into the unknown. But there’s an arguably even more mysterious frontier hidden beneath us. Nowhere is that more real than at Challenger Deep. The deepest known point on Earth, Challenger Deep is located in the 1,580-mile-long Mariana Trench at the floor of the Pacific Ocean. Getting to the bottom of this ancient chasm means diving more than 6.8 miles (around 36,000 feet) underwater. For a sense of scale, Mount Everest could be dropped into this chasm, and its summit still wouldn’t reach the surface.

That absurd depth and bone-crushing pressure make Challenger Deep brutally difficult to study. As a result, assumptions about what lies down there rarely hold up for long. Scientists long believed the area’s frigid, pitch-dark depths couldn’t sustain life, until a pair of divers reported animals near the seafloor in 1960. Now, a team using a robotic submersible in the trench indicates they have found the deepest evidence of explosive volcanic eruptions ever documented in the ocean.

Industry observers note that using the remotely operated Jason/Medea submarine robot, the team documented evidence of pyroclastic rocks (the shattered debris of violent eruptions) on the trench wall some 20,000 feet below the surface. Finding those kinds of rocks there was unexpected and will change the way geologists view the area. Writing today in the journal Frontiers in Earth Science, the researchers say their discoveries may also “help explain why the Challenger Deep is so deep.”.

“Explosive volcanism near trenches is unusual, so we were very surprised,” Dr. Robert J. Stern, a geologist at the University of Texas at Dallas and study co-author, mentioned in a statement. “These are the deepest pyroclastic rocks documented to date from anywhere in the ocean.”.

Reaching the depth needed to study the Mariana Trench takes some serious equipment and preparation. In 2012, Titanic director James Cameron famously made the dive with a specially designed submersible that reportedly cost around $10 million to build. In this case, the team of scientists turned to a veteran robotic system called Jason/Medea. Part of the National Deep Submergence Facility and funded by the National Science Foundation, Jason/Medea traces its earliest version back to 1988. From the outside, the ROV somewhat resembles a Zamboni machine used to surface ice skating rinks.

The robot can operate as deep as 21,385 feet below the surface, thanks to a roughly six-mile long fiber-optic cable connecting it to a vessel on the surface. Jason is equipped with a video and still-imaging systems. Its footage travels up through Medea, a companion robot that  hangs slightly higher in the water to buffer Jason from the motion of the vessel above. In addition to taking photos and videos, Jason has mechanical arms he can use to collect rock and sediment samples. The robotic duo has completed hundreds of dives around the world, analyzing hydrothermal vents in the Atlantic and Pacific Ocean, and even visiting a 1,600-year-old sunken Roman trading ship.

Industry observers note that in this case, the scientists deployed their robot companion in late 2024 along a 341 mile segment of the trench near Challenger Deep. Over seven dives, the robot team covered around 186 miles, taking photos and videos along the way. Analyzing the footage, the human team determined that the eastern part of the stretch is deeper than the western part and has steeper trench walls. They came across the old volcanic rocks on that steeper western side, seen below arranged in a thin flat layer. Exactly where these rocks erupted from remains unclear.

Industry observers note that ”We haven’t identified the eruption sites yet,” Stern added. “We know that these hot pyroclastic flows moved down slopes, but we don’t think they moved very far. They retained enough heat to re-weld themselves into pretty hard rocks, and that heat would’ve been lost if the pyroclastic flows traveled great distances.”.

The unexpected rocks were only one part of the expedition. The team also set out to study fragments of older, exposed crust and mantle. They also tasked the robot with studying the Shinaki Seep Field, one of deepest known hydrothermal vents sites on the planet. There was some cleanup duty as well:  the team recovered fluid-sampling devices left behind by a previous group of Japanese scientists in 2016. Explorers have rather glibly documented human trash all the way down at the bottom of Challenger Deep but these scientists, at least, won’t be adding to the litter.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that battlefield 6 is about to receive a new update.
  • That honour goes to a couple of the high-level changes Battlefield Studios has included with the upcoming patch, which range from a major pass on audio to a fix for a particularly annoying bug that’s been seemingly introduced with a recent patch.
  • Thew newly introduced content takes the form of a limited-time version of the game’s Empire State map, which covers it in snow and tweaks its layout slightly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that battlefield 6 is about to receive a new update. Version 1.1.3.0 is set to arrive tomorrow, December 9 to kick off the third and final phase of the game’s first season. Winter Offensive brings some holiday-themed new content to the game, but it’s not the most interesting part of the patch.

That honour goes to a couple of the high-level changes Battlefield Studios has included with the upcoming patch, which range from a major pass on audio to a fix for a particularly annoying bug that’s been seemingly introduced with a recent patch.

Thew newly introduced content takes the form of a limited-time version of the game’s Empire State map, which covers it in snow and tweaks its layout slightly. To go along with that there are new limited-time modes for both multiplayer and Redsec’s Gauntlet. The event mode will be available in Conquest, and Domination.

The Ice Climbing Axe is the only newly introduced weapon in this drop. The battle pass gets a new Winter Offensive bonus path, just like we’ve seen with previous seasonal stages. This is how you unlock the axe, too.

Easily the most interesting change in this patch is the range of improvements to audio across the board. First, footstep audio received a massive pass that should make it easier to hear enemy footsteps, easier to locate them, and across different surfaces.

Sources indicate that some of the bugs that caused certain sounds to simply vanish have been fixed. This was especially prevalent in battle royale matches. BF Studios explained in the patch notes that it has adjusted memory priorities for in-game sounds in order to prioritise the most crucial ones. This is not the end of the road on audio, however, as the developer continues to work on making the soundscape more stable and reliable.

Some of those audio changes are the result of recent testing done in Battlefield Labs, which is also responsible for another exciting addition in this latest patch: improvements to hit registration.

While BF6 has had solid and stable netcode, certain situations would sometimes create uncertainty about how you died, and why certain actions seemingly failed to perform at that particular moment.

The focus in this enhancement is to improve the reliability of how actions in close-quarter combat are translated, which includes firing before fully going into ADS, quick aim changes and more.

Speaking of close-range, the patch also brings another pass to soldier visibility to make it easier for enemies to stand out from the background. This is particularly relevant in areas with low contrast, or busy environments with lots of particle and visual effects.

Sources indicate that 1.1.3.0 also brings yet another set of weapon handling and gunplay tweaks, this time focusing on accuracy problems with first shots. You can also expect more tweaks to attachment behaviour with regards to recoil.

Something else worth highlighting is that vehicle gameplay is getting several smaller tweaks that have to do with how they interact with the world, how their HUDs behave and more. Finally, your settings should no longer be reset after applying an update. BF Studios indicates there are still some instances where that might happen, but the concern should be fixed for the majority of players.

You can read the full change log on the Battlefield blog.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hailey Bieber is sharing her experience with premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), a condition she indicates has fueled her growing interest in women’s health research.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hailey Bieber is sharing her experience with premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), a condition she indicates has fueled her growing interest in women’s health research.

The Rhode Beauty founder recently unveiled a $5 million, three-year partnership with the Foundation for Women’s Health in an interview with Women’s Wear Daily (WWD).

“As a woman, I feel frustrated by the lack of research, the lack of awareness, the lack of certain conversation around it,” Bieber told WWD.

Industry observers note that motherhood has also shaped her perspective. Bieber welcomed her son, Jack Blues, with her husband, Justin Bieber, in 2024, describing the experience as a “really intense and special journey.”.

She also shared that she “struggled” with PMDD after giving birth, noting that there’s “not a lot of conversation or research around it.”.

“When we can identify with each other and have conversations relating to each other and talking about the things we’re dealing with and struggling with, I do think it makes it feel like less of a lonely journey,” Bieber stated.

PMDD is a complexcondition that causes severe physical and psychological symptoms that typically occur in the days or weeks leading up to menstruation.

“What distinguishes PMDD from the more common PMS (premenstrual syndrome) is the severity of the symptoms and how significantly they can interfere with daily functioning,” Sari Eitches, MD, dual board certified physician and medical advisor to Terra Mare, told Healthline.

“Another defining feature is the timing: symptoms typically worsen in the week or two before a period, resolve within a few days after menstruation begins, and are minimal or absent during the rest of the cycle,” she said.

Eitches also noted that PMDD is a chronic condition that can affect women at any stage of their reproductive lives, from adolescence through perimenopause, as long as they are having menstrual cycles.

“It is caused by a sensitivity to cyclic hormonal and neurotransmitter fluctuations, so [it] can occur in anyone with a menstrual cycle, though stages of hormonal fluctuation- including postpartum, weaning breastfeeding, and perimenopause- can be a trigger,” she added.

According to research published in 2024, approximately 1.6% of women and girls meet the strict diagnostic criteria for PMDD, equivalent to an estimated 31 million people worldwide.

A higher percentage of 3.2% have a provisional diagnosis, meaning a healthcare professional may believe a person has PMDD, but symptoms have not been measured for a sustained amount of time to meet the criteria for a confirmed diagnosis.

Eitches said that women with a personal or family history of depression or anxiety may be more prone to developing PMDD, as are women with a family history of PMDD itself.

It has been revealed that “PMDD is understood to be caused by a combination of heritable biological sensitivities and environmental triggers. These can include a history of trauma, chronic stress, and other chronic medical conditions,” she noted.

Eitches also said that you should consider seeing a doctor if your symptoms are severe enough that they’re interfering with your ability to go to work or school, maintain your relationships, or participate in your life in the same way that you do during the other weeks of the month.

Sources indicate that to diagnose PMDD, a healthcare professional will review your medical history and symptoms and may perform a physical exam. They will typically ask you to track your symptoms over at least two menstrual cycles.

A PMDD diagnosis generally requires at least five symptoms, including at least one mood-related symptom, that occur before menstruation, improve shortly after a period begins, and significantly interfere with daily life.

Treatment options for PMDD include prescription medications and over-the-counter treatments that may help relieve certain symptoms, such as:.

Eitches noted that cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) can also help manage symptoms.

Lifestyle changes may also help manage PMDD symptoms, including practicing relaxation techniques, eating a balanced diet, limiting sugary and salty foods, and getting regular physical activity.

Eitches noted that getting enough high quality sleep and resting on a consistent schedule is also notable.

“I also recommend focusing on a whole-foods-based diet, limiting added sugar and caffeine, and avoiding cigarette smoking,” she said.

Fancy axes and simple pottery show how interconnected Europe was 5,000 years ago

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (538 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, the Rhine River stands as a physical border between parts of France and Germany, and a cultural boundary between Western and Central Europe.
  • It has been revealed that sebastian Schultrich, an archaeologist at Kiel University in Germany, looked at late Neolithic coarse pottery, double axes, and collective graves from either side of the Rhine and found significant cross-boundary ties in the late 4th and early 3rd millennia BCE.
  • “The combination of pottery, burial rituals and tools reveals new insights into life 5,000 years ago,” Schultrich stated in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, the Rhine River stands as a physical border between parts of France and Germany, and a cultural boundary between Western and Central Europe. This physical and cultural separation seems to have existed for a very long time. Archaeological evidence on either side of the river as early as the late fourth millennia BCE reveals differences. Archaeologists have determined that the river is a sort of barrier during this time—but new research challenges this conclusion.

It has been revealed that sebastian Schultrich, an archaeologist at Kiel University in Germany, looked at late Neolithic coarse pottery, double axes, and collective graves from either side of the Rhine and found significant cross-boundary ties in the late 4th and early 3rd millennia BCE. His findings, described in a study recently published in the archaeological journal Germania, suggest that populations in Western, Central, and Northern Europe were more connected than previously assumed.

“The combination of pottery, burial rituals and tools reveals new insights into life 5,000 years ago,” Schultrich stated in a statement.

Recent findings suggest that the pottery in question, called coarse ware, is simple and plain—so much so that archaeologists have seen it as culturally insignificant. The roughly-shaped artifacts have emerged in many regions of Europe. It became widespread in modern-day central and northern France as well as the western Alpine region starting in the mid-4th millennium BCE. Afterward, it also became prominent in modern-day western and northern Germany and Denmark.

Sources indicate that “There are indications that a convergence of pottery styles across such great distances occurred gradually and unconsciously. This is an indicator of high mobility within a region where there were no distinct barriers between groups, or where the boundaries were fluid,” said Schultrich.

Double stone axes—prestigious axes with two cutting edges and a shaft hole—were also widespread in this period. Archaeologists have discovered them from France through Central Europe to Scandinavia and Poland. While the dates of the French double stone axes has been a subject of contention, it’s currently clear that they, along with the Central and Northern European versions, hail from the the 4th and early 3rd millennia BCE. Unlike coarse ware, the double axe design seems to have been intentionally widespread, showing that a shared concept existed on either side of the river.

Recent findings suggest that the same regions are also home to different versions of large-scale group burials, including passage graves or gallery graves. But they all were the final resting place of dozens to hundreds of individuals, were used over many generations, and were the locations of ritual acts and gatherings. This is more evidence of a shared idea, even though its regional manifestation differed.

Recent findings suggest that “It was not a uniform cultural complex,” Schultrich explained. “What we see here is a network characterised by fundamental narratives, yet one that simultaneously allowed scope for strong regional peculiarities. This is an early example of a complex, differentiated form of society in which identity combined both supra-regional and local elements.”.

By drawing prehistoric connections across the Rhine, Schultrich revealed ties across late Neolithic Europe that clearly overcame the watery boundary.

It’s clear that the developer is committed to the free-to-play action RPG, and the game’s recent success on Steam, and PlayStation has more than likely solidified the team’s plans for the future of the game.

On the official Where Winds Meet account on Twitter, the developer shared a brief roadmap of some of what we can expect over the course of December. The roadmap is split into the four weeks of the month, covering everything from smaller quests to more larger additions.

The first week started off a little light, with two new Jianghu Legacy Quests: Twelve Years of Feuds, and An Unholy Prophecy. Both quests are currently available in the game.

According to recent reports, the biggest addition, of course, is the newly introduced Roarding Sands region, which becomes available the same day as the RPG’s global launch on mobile devices during the second week. Roarding Sands arrives December 11, along with a new campaign boss dubbed River Master.

The third and fourth weeks of the month bring us the Scarlet Shock Sword Trial, as well as the fresh Blazing Gale Dance Hero’s Realm activity. Where Winds meet wraps it all up on December 30 with the Fireworks Festival.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.

Such a hard decision to choose the next novel for this blog! But in this current dark world we all need some gentler moments, and Ann Patchett’s latest novel WHISTLER will give you many of those along with much food for reflection.

In a recent development, patchett is one of America’s best known novelists and since 2004 when I read her memoir TRUTH AND BEAUTY, the story of her 20 year friendship with Lucy Grealy, whose incredible book AUTOBIOGRAPHY OF A FACE I read around the same time, I have read all of Patchett's novels. Lucy died of a heroin overdose when she was 39 after almost a lifetime of struggle with the aftermath of having a large part of her jaw removed when she was nine. I have early editions of both these beautiful memoirs on my bookshelf and although I haven’t read them for over twenty years I still remember their emotional impact.

Ann Patchett has continued to write memorable books, mostly novels, and now in her early 60s gives every indication that we will be able to look forward to many more. She is also well-known for her support of writers and books and is the co-founder of the bookstore Parnassus Books in Nashville where she lives. Her stance on social media is refreshing; she watches no television, does not have a cell phone and doesn’t participate in any form of social media. However, on her website you can find her interviewing authors and talking about books although she never watches those video clips! What she does do of course is read, write novels, and support all things books. Perhaps a recipe more of us should follow, at least occasionally!

Sources indicate that here is the back-of-the-book description of WHISTLER, published in June 2026. On Goodreads it currently has over 290,000 ratings and over 334,00 reviews with an average score of 4.28/5. So many of you have likely already read it!

The acclaimed, prize-winning #1 New York Times bestselling writer returns with a moving, luminous novel that reminds us of the sweetness and impermanence of life and the power of connection to defy time.When Daphne Fuller and her husband Jonathan visit the Metropolitan Museum of Art, they notice an older, white-haired gentleman following them. The man turns out to be Eddie Triplett, her former stepfather, who had been married to her mother for a little more than year when Daphne was nine. Now fifty-three, Daphne hasn’t seen Eddie for many years, not since the fateful event that changed the direction of both their lives. Meeting again, time falls away; while their relationship was brief, it had a profound impact on them both, and now that they are reunited, they have no intention of ever being separated again.Whistler is a story about two adults looking back over the choices they made, and the choices that were made for them. It’s a story about bravery, memory, the often small yet consequential moments that define our lives, and the endless stream of loss that in time comes for us all. Beautiful in its simplicity, it is ultimately about how love endures, and how the feeling of being known by one other person, even for a short period of time, can change everything.

A novel with a horse on the cover and perhaps with a description like this may seem like a novel for women. And of course it is, but I think both women and men could find this an immersive and so very pleasurable read. A story about aging and memory, and how our brains filter and rewrite our personal histories as the years roll by, it is also about those childhood memories we may have forgotten because they were so very fleeting.

In a recent development, the story revolves around the relationship between Daphne and Eddie; a relationship that occupied only one year of Daphne’s life when she was a child, and ended abruptly when she and Eddie, at that time her stepfather, both escaped death following a car accident. So when Daphne, now aged 53, saw Eddie again and they renewed their relationship, they both come to understand how influential their short relationship was on their lives. And as a reader you might find yourself thinking about brief relationships you had as a child that changed the trajectory of your life in ways that were profound but that perhaps you have not thought about very much. Of course some children are the victims of childhood trauma, but in this case Daphne and Eddie’s relationship changed both their lives and Daphne’s life in particular in positive ways.

So many news items are about traumatic and exploitative relationships, but what about the positive ones? The teacher who believed in you? The older cousin who took the time to listen? The best friend who you shared so much with but who you’ve not seen or contacted in thirty years? What are those memories? How has your mind stored them, preserved them, incorporated them into your life, your belief systems? Likely if you could go back and view them as they happened you would discover that they have been distorted over time, but perhaps this doesn’t matter, at least when you are content with the memory. In Whistler it becomes clear that Daphne and Eddie’s memories of the accident they were in are not the same, but that Eddie’s brief presence in Daphne’s life made a profound difference to the evolution of her resilience and bravery.

Often our favorite stories are about close family relationships, especially mothers and daughters, or sibling relationships. Whistler is about both of those, but also about the less-explored psychological dynamics of step-parenting and non-traditional family structures, and most especially good ones. The step-parent so often has that ‘wicked step mother’ or ‘abusive step father’ vibe but what about all the wonderful step parents?

And then there is Whistler, the horse. You will need to read the book to discover that story!
